items.title: Attrition Pocket
items.content:
“The two most powerful warriors are patience and time.” – Leo Tolstoy
 In 1983, the Soviet Union began constructing the 4,100-foot-long Southern Bridge in Ukraine’s capital city of Kyiv. Also known locally as the Pivdennyi Bridge, the span opened to road traffic in 1990 and metro service in 1992—years that bookend Ukraine’s declaration of independence in the messy aftermath of the Soviet Union’s collapse. As one of a handful of large bridges crossing the Dnipro River—a majestic expanse that runs the full length of Ukraine from north to south, effectively cutting the country in two—the structure is of outsized importance to military planners on both sides of the war:
 “ Almost everything that comes in from Ukraine’s western partners, from shells and missiles to armoured vehicles and fuel, must eventually cross the river to reach the front in the east. 
 Kyiv sits at the heart of this system. The main rail and road routes from the west converge here, while routes from the left bank fan out towards Chernihiv, Sumy, Poltava and Kharkiv. The capital is therefore both a gateway for Western aid and a rear base for operations to the north and east. ”

 Ties that bind | Mostobud 
 Since the earliest weeks of the war in 2022, hardliners within Russia have at times demanded to know why Moscow declined to destroy these crucial logistical links. Some speculated that the bridges were harder to destroy than many understood, while others lamented Russian President Vladimir Putin’s soft touch in his prosecution of the conflict. A month ago, it became clear that the Kremlin had decided the time was finally ripe for a change in tactics :
 “ Russia struck a bridge linking two sides ​of the Ukrainian capital Kyiv for the second successive day, officials said on Friday, part of an intensifying campaign of air attacks on infrastructure ‌that is upending daily life. 
 An evening drone strike on the closed Southern Bridge was the latest in a series of attacks since Thursday that forced the full or partial suspension of traffic across it and two other bridges spanning the vast Dnipro River. ”

 Cutting the ties | Reuters 
 In the ensuing weeks, continued attacks on a number of Dnipro bridges have been reported in open sources, executed with a combination of advanced drones, powerful missiles, and even bombs dropped from Russian aircraft. Official confirmation of the impact of this escalation is understandably difficult to come by, but judging from the worried commentary emerging from unofficial Ukrainian channels, the complete severing of the major bridges would indeed present a serious challenge for the armies fighting Russia on the eastern front.
 Under the premise that Putin is more cunning and sinister than dovish and tepid, and broadening the framework of analysis from the war in Ukraine to the larger global conflict that includes the war against Iran, we have developed an alternative explanation for why Russia waited so long to split Ukraine in two. If we are right, it foretells an imminent climax to what we have modeled as World War III.

items.title: Recycle Bin
items.content:
“To create greater convergence, we need more integration.” – Emmanuel Macron
 The global energy behemoth that is the US natural gas industry continues its relentless growth, making a mockery of pessimistic forecasters. One struggles to properly frame the awesome scale of what is transpiring for a lay audience, but let’s try: In 2026, the US is forecast to grow natural gas production by more than the combined total output of the entire European Union (EU). In 2027, it is anticipated to do so again. Appalachian supply is so abundant that spot prices are running at roughly $1-2 per million BTUs, or $6-12 per barrel of oil on an energy-equivalent basis—less than the daily price swing on Brent crude contracts during these turbulent times.

 Huge bounty | EIA 
 In addition to driving wild improvements in drilling technology, these cutthroat prices are also compelling a wave of industry consolidation. Last week, EQT—a company we expect to profile in November’s Pro Tier deep dive—announced its intent to gobble up one of its pure-play competitors:
 “ EQT’s acquisition of rival producer ​Range Resources this week marks the latest consolidation in the natural gas industry, as producers are scrambling to lock in supply to feed growing ‌demand for liquefied natural gas exports and power demand. 
 Canonsburg, Pennsylvania-based EQT said on Monday it will buy Fort Worth, Texas-based Range Resources in a $13 billion all-stock deal that will create the nation’s biggest gas producer. EQT is the second-largest natural gas producer in the US… 
 The deal underscores how top US gas producers are racing to consolidate ahead of what ⁠they expect will be a step-change in domestic demand, driven by new LNG [liquefied natural gas] export terminals coming online and a buildout of gas-fired power plants to supply electricity-hungry data centers—even as a near-term glut has depressed prices and forced operators to curtail output. ”

 Big business | EQT 
 There is little doubt that gas demand for LNG-exporting magic machines will materialize, and progress on the wave of new terminals being thrown up along the US Gulf Coast can be tracked closely. Whether the electricity-hungry data centers get built is another question, and confidence in the bankability of those future flows was undoubtedly shaken by the rout in artificial intelligence (AI) equities last week.
 One gating factor for fulfilling data center demand is a chronic shortage of the gas-fired power turbines required to convert the fuel into electricity. The major suppliers of these sophisticated contraptions are sold out for years, with some reports stating that new orders placed today won’t be filled until 2030. Even some delivery slots for 2032 are being snapped up. In the grand AI race, time is often more important than money, and without the engines available to burn abundant natural gas supplies, the volumes of shale gas coming online might remain excessive.
 Unless, of course, alternatives can be found to fill the demand gap more quickly. Might old engines do the trick? As it turns out, there are tens of thousands of used aircraft engines on planes and in hangars the world over, and—with varying degrees of effort, time, and money—these workhorses can be repurposed for the task. Let’s head to the airport and learn why flying is about to become even more expensive.

items.title: Gating Functions
items.content:
“We’re celebrating the greatest oil victory in history. To the victor belong the spoils, right?” – Donald J. Trump
 In the late summer of 2021, heavy oil production in Venezuela’s Orinoco Belt temporarily crashed by 25%. The proximate cause of the decline was the need to divert lighter grades of domestically produced crude to the country’s struggling refineries. Those lighter hydrocarbons would normally have been used as diluents to enable transporting Orinoco’s otherwise solid-like oil sludges to markets near and far. Absent the lights, production of the heavies had to be curtailed.

 Black goo | Bloomberg 
 The root cause of the mini-crisis was the cumulative effect of years of suffocating sanctions levied against Venezuela by successive US administrations that made external sourcing of materials, capital goods, and investor money progressively more difficult. In the final weeks of 2025, such financial weapons were supplemented with floating ones, as the US Navy imposed a partial blockade of oil tankers into and out of the beleaguered country. Among those inbound, a few that of Russian origin found themselves in a particularly interesting showdown :
 “ A tanker subject to US sanctions carrying some 300,000 barrels of naphtha from Russia entered Venezuelan waters late on Thursday, while another began redirecting course in the Atlantic Ocean, ship tracking data showed, a reflection of diverging last-minute decisions by ship owners after President Donald Trump ordered a ‘blockade’ of oil tankers under sanctions bound for the OPEC country earlier this week. 
 The move ramped up pressure on Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro by targeting the country’s main source of income and followed the seizure by the US of an oil tanker off the coast of Venezuela earlier in December. ”
 The naphtha en route from Russia was itself meant to serve as diluent, and Venezuela’s inability to source it in sufficient quantities was once again contributing to precipitously falling production. The escalating pressure campaign that followed culminated in the US Army’s elite Delta Force successfully snatching President Nicolás Maduro in early January, a jarring inflection point in the long-standing geopolitical skirmish between the two countries.

 Heavy stuff | Getty 
 Maduro’s abrupt departure left behind a government that was more pliant to US President Donald Trump’s demands. Much of the sanctions pressure exited with the former strongman, and the flow of diluent in and heavy crude out rebounded markedly. According to a recent report delivered to acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez last week, oil production reached a remarkable 1.25 million barrels per day (bpd)—up from a low of just 830,000 bpd in December—due to higher production in the Orinoco Belt and conventional crude production gains.
 If one closely examines the political and molecular mayhem that has so characterized the Venezuelan oil industry over the past decade, powerful evidence emerges for many of the core themes regularly argued in these pages. Included among them are proof of the shifting molecular definition of oil itself, a proper ranking of politics ahead of geology in the hierarchy of constraints on oil production, and—perhaps most importantly—a window into the true hydrocarbon potential of the Western Hemisphere. Let’s head to Caracas to explore each in order.

items.title: Tough Comp
items.content:
“Measure what is measurable, and make measurable what is not so.” – Galileo Galilei
 Roughly two and a half years ago, we published “ Mapping the War ,” a guide to following the daily ebbs and flows of the war between NATO and Russia over Ukraine. In it, we listed several accessible open-source social media accounts that, despite their known biases, provided good signal in a sea of propagandistic noise.
 One account profiled was the Military Summary channel on YouTube , an excellent source of real-time information that has collectively garnered more than 400 million views worldwide. By consuming the channel’s twice-daily, bite-sized summaries of the war, we became aware of several important developments long before they made headlines in the Financial Times or Washington Post . Among them were Ukraine’s huge assault on Russian cargo and tanker ships in the Sea of Azov in July, Russia’s retaliation by blockading Ukraine’s Black Sea ports and destroying Odesa’s port infrastructure, and countless other escalations.

 Put your likes | Military Summary 
 One thing that stands out after watching hundreds of such episodes over the years is just how tough it is to inflict a knockout blow from the air using only long-range, standoff munitions. Consider Russia’s years-long campaign against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Russia has fired thousands of highly advanced ballistic missiles and tens of thousands of cutting-edge drones in a seemingly relentless daily campaign, but only now, with Kyiv effectively out of air-defense missiles, is the target deteriorating at a truly alarming rate.
 If you live in Britain, you have probably been told that this pace exists because Russia is a paper tiger whose missiles don’t shoot straight, or Russian President Vladimir Putin has cancer (did you see his hands twitch?), or his agents are too busy Q-Tipping your local politician’s bidet to focus on winning the war. In the rest of the world, the natural conclusion is that it is prohibitively difficult to inflict sufficient damage from afar to force capitulation, especially against a country as large and as clearly motivated to fight as Ukraine.

 What a weirdo | The Telegraph 
 Against such a backdrop, breaking news published in the Wall Street Journal over the weekend piqued our interest:
 “ American warships in the Middle East are preparing for an escalation in fighting in case President Trump opts for a fresh round of attacks against Iran in the coming weeks, according to US officials familiar with the planning. 
 During a rare visit to a US aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer operating in the Arabian Sea, The Wall Street Journal observed flight operations, as well as a significant replenishment of munitions and supplies—including a large delivery of standoff land attack missiles and bunker-buster bombs designed to penetrate ground targets. ”
 Given Iran’s credible threats to unleash an extraordinarily violent response to any renewed strikes on its territory, just what, exactly, are US President Donald Trump and his advisers hoping to accomplish with yet another round of fighting? Is a civilization-ending knockout blow to Iran even remotely possible using a couple of aircraft carriers, some long-range bombers taking off stateside, and what remains of American air bases in the Middle East? Can we learn anything from how challenging it has been for Russia to deal such a blow to Ukraine, despite sharing a border more than 1,000 miles long and enjoying access to its entire formidable military-industrial complex for the task?
 A direct comparison between Iran and Ukraine is not only readily available using open sources, but the numbers will come as a sobering shock. Let’s have a look.

items.title: Margin Call
items.content:
“We choose mania over boredom every time.” – James Gleick
 In late August, the Errea Wittu arrived in Guyanese waters. The floating production, storage, and offloading (FPSO) magic oil boat will join four others already extracting hydrocarbons from the Stabroek Block, Big Oil’s glistening crown jewel du jour . Once full operations begin in December, total production in Guyana will reach more than one million barrels per day (bpd), or roughly one barrel for every resident of that formerly impoverished nation. This is up from no barrels less than a decade ago.
 For all the withering criticism the government of Guyana received from the keep-it-in-the-ground climate crowd over the allegedly one-sided nature of the deal it cut with Stabroek’s operator, ExxonMobil, the country has transformed from one of the world’s poorest to one of its fastest-growing economies almost overnight. According to the International Monetary Fund , the country’s real GDP was just $5.5 billion in 2020. It grew 20% the next year, followed by an astonishing 63% the year after. In 2023, 2024, and 2025, the Guyanese economy swelled another 34%, 44%, and 19%, respectively. By the time it exited 2025, GDP had reached $27 billion, a fivefold increase in just five years.
 And 2026? The IMF estimates another 22% .

 One king | Getty 
 As invariably happens when the champagne fizz of treasure is uncorked, neighboring regions have received some of the spillover: A race to drill in the waters off Suriname has yielded respectable results. Although not yet on par with the heady bounty of Stabroek, the GranMorgu development in Block 58 will soon be home to an FPSO of its own, with production of 220,000 bpd targeted for mid-2028.
 If two points make a line, it is not all that difficult to grab a ruler and extend it a little farther east, and the success achieved in one part of the Equatorial Atlantic geological realm has sparked renewed interest in the Equatorial Margin off Brazil’s northern coast. Long known to have significant oil potential, the area has primarily been subject to drilling in the shallower waters closer to shore. A history of spotty results and fierce opposition from environmentalists to further exploration dampened industry enthusiasm for the area’s prospects.

 Blue marks the spot? | Tenaris 
 In mid-August, Petrobras, the state-controlled integrated oil and gas company of Brazil, rekindled interest in the area after announcing preliminary results from its latest exploration work:
 “ The results of one of Brazil’s most anticipated wells in years show that it contains hydrocarbons in a deepwater area offshore the state of Amapá, according to Petrobras, which is the sole owner and operator of the exploration block. 
 The Morpho-1 well is located in Block FZA-M-59, more than 100 miles offshore and 300 miles from the mouth of the Amazon River, within Brazil’s Equatorial Margin. Petrobras hopes the frontier region will become its next major source of oil and gas production as output from the country’s prolific pre-salt basins gradually matures. 
 Petrobras said the well was drilled in a water depth of almost 9,500 ft, and the presence of hydrocarbons was confirmed through well logs. The company did not release further details about the quality of the discovery. ”
 By October, the company had discovered an additional oil-bearing layer in the same block, adding to the excitement.
 As often happens in the early days of a potentially significant find, some are cautioning against prematurely drawing definitive conclusions. Given the stakes involved—and the fact that Brazil’s near-term political future will be decided in the hotly contested presidential runoff election tomorrow—there’s no better time to head south and have a look for ourselves. Will the Equatorial Margin soon become as consequential for the industry as Stabroek? Let’s hazard a guess.

items.title: Diesel of Discontent
items.content:
“There are three things in the world that deserve no mercy: hypocrisy, fraud, and tyranny.” – Frederick William Robertson
 During the first six months of 2026, European buyers gorged on practically every liquefied natural gas (LNG) cargo Russia’s Yamal plant could produce. Of the 140 ships that set sail from that facility, 136 offloaded their life-nourishing bounty in Europe, with France, Belgium, Spain, and the Netherlands quietly absorbing the bulk. Analysts estimate the revenue generated from these sales to be on the order of $7 billion—funds that were presumably funneled to President Vladimir Putin’s war machine, which is either on the brink of total collapse or fixing to march all the way to Paris, depending on which side of their mouths European leaders are lecturing from today.
 In May, British Prime Minister Keir Starmer—suffocating on terrible poll numbers and staring down the barrel of a diesel and jet fuel crisis of his own—enraged London’s spreadsheet dwellers by daring to carve out a sanctions exception allowing imports of Russian crude refined in India. Despite the firestorm, the exception remains, and a full accounting of just how much shadow diesel has made its way to His Majesty’s islands is unlikely to adorn the front pages of the Financial Times anytime soon.
 In perusing the hyperbolic coverage that has followed US President Donald Trump’s now-infamous dirty diesel deal with Putin, we find little acknowledgment of these glaring bits of hypocrisy. Take this missive from Politico , which sought commentary from various European Union leaders en route to whatever meaningless talking session they might have been attending on Monday morning:
 “ On their way into their meeting, the EU’s foreign ministers remained united in their insistence that increasing pressure on Moscow was the only way forward. 
 ‘Obviously our position has not changed — pressure on Russia, sanctions, support to Ukraine, Russia’s isolation is the way to peace,’ Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said. 
 The British Foreign Office’s minister of state Stephen Doughty said London was ‘not planning to follow suit with’ purchasing Russian energy and would ratchet up ‘economic pressure’ on Moscow. ”

 In her natural habitat | Getty 
 None of this is to excuse how Trump put himself in this position, of course. His failure to end the war in Ukraine swiftly upon taking office and the disastrous decision to go to war with Iran have compounded error upon error, and there is a direct line between these broken campaign promises and the electoral pickle in which he currently finds himself. His half-hearted return to his correct instinct that high energy prices make for bad politics might be a classic example of too little, too late, but late is still undefeated in the battle against never.

 Regrettable circumstances | Getty 
 As we have been arguing since April of 2022, the West’s entire approach to economic war against Putin’s Russia was fatally flawed from the start, doomed to the predictable loop of failures being experienced now. There is a better way, one that would breathe much-needed economic air into an anemic European economy, raise global standards of living from their current downward trajectory, and substantially ramp up real economic pressure against Redmanbad in Moscow. Let’s revisit the details.
